response: {"text":"The study examined how speakers of a certain language modify their speech when addressing people who know little or none of that language. Four separate investigations were carried out: first, a look at how this simplified style shows up in popular written works; second, a survey of native speakers' gut feelings about the way they talk to outsiders; third, a close look at real‑life street encounters where a passerby asked for directions; and fourth, an analysis of conversations between non‑native speakers and officials who regularly interact with them. The findings showed that the simplified style is fairly common, but its frequency changes a lot depending on the setting and the particular exchange. People tend to believe that speakers drop certain word orders, use base verb forms instead of conjugated ones, replace weak pronouns with stronger ones, and omit linking verbs, subject pronouns and small function words. Actual speech, especially from those who often deal with foreigners, only partly matches these beliefs, and many of the changes are strongly linked to the specific situation. Some of the patterns also resemble those found in other languages, hinting at universal tendencies to simplify speech when communicating with non‑native listeners."}
